context_blurb:
Every living thing on Earth is related: a bat, a whale, a horse and you all descend, with changes, from shared ancestors. This common descent is settled science, and fossils, the bones of limbs, embryos and leftover body parts all show it.

Fossils fall in the order descent predicts: fish appear more than 500 million years ago, the first mammals about 225 million and rabbits, which are mammals, about 55 million. So a rabbit in rock older than the first fish would break that order outright, for mammals descend from fish-like ancestors. The biologist J. B. S. Haldane is said to have named Precambrian rabbits, in rock over about 539 million years old, as a find that would shake his belief in evolution; none has turned up.

Fish with fleshy, lobed fins are known from rock about 380 million years old, and the first four-legged animals from rock about 365 million. So Neil Shubin's team searched the Canadian Arctic in stream-laid rock from about 375 million years ago, laid down as fish were moving onto land. In 2004 it found Tiktaalik, a transitional fossil: a fish with scales and gills, yet also a neck, and arm and wrist bones in its fins. Reptiles come only tens of millions of years later.

Archaeopteryx turned up in 1861, two years after Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species. It had a bird's feathers and wings, but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long tail of bone, like small theropods, the mostly meat-eating dinosaurs. In 1868 Thomas Huxley compared it with fossil reptiles and argued that birds descend from small, meat-eating dinosaurs. Birds are now counted as the last living theropods.

Whales once walked. In 1981 Philip Gingerich and Donald Russell named Pakicetus, a wolf-sized mammal from northern Pakistan that ran on four slender legs about 50 million years ago. Its ear bones, unusually thick and dense, mark it as a whale, a feature all later whales inherited from a shared ancestor. Ambulocetus then paddled with webbed hind feet, and Basilosaurus lived wholly at sea on tiny hind legs.

A cat's foreleg, a whale's flipper, a bat's wing and your arm run, swim, fly and grasp, yet each has one upper-arm bone, a pair of forearm bones, then wrist bones and fingers. Parts matched bone for bone, whatever their job, are homologous. Richard Owen, who gave homology its meaning in biology in 1843, read the shared build as an ideal plan in the Creator's mind. Charles Darwin argued instead that all four were inherited from one shared ancestor, each line reshaping the old limb for its own way of life. Indeed all four-legged animals' forelegs, a lizard's as much as a horse's, are homologous, inherited from an ancestor of them all. Parts that share a job but not a build, like a bat's wing and an insect's boneless one, are analogous: they arose separately.

Every backboned embryo, an animal at its earliest stage, from a shark's to yours, grows a row of ridges at its throat called pharyngeal arches; a fish turns most into the frames of its gills. In a human the same arches build parts of the jaw, the middle ear and the throat. A human embryo never has working gills. The arches are a homology, inherited from an ancestor fish and people share.

Ernst Haeckel's drawings of 1874 showed five early embryos, from a fish to a human, almost alike. He had exaggerated, adding or leaving out features and fudging sizes. In 1997 Michael Richardson and his colleagues photographed real embryos of many backboned animals: the embryos differ more than Haeckel's drawings show. Yet real embryos do share pharyngeal arches and a tail, and in 1998 Richardson wrote that on a fundamental level Haeckel was correct. Haeckel's belief that embryos replay their ancestors' adult forms is long abandoned.

A vestigial part has lost the main job it did for the animal's ancestors. A grown whale keeps a pair of small hip bones, not joined to the spine, and its embryo starts hind limb buds that then stop: leftovers of the legs its ancestors walked on. Its hip bones still anchor mating muscles, so they are vestigial yet not useless. Your coccyx, or tailbone, is all that remains of the tail a human embryo grows and loses between its fourth and eighth weeks. Pelvic-floor muscles anchor to it, but it does no tail's work, so it is still vestigial: vestigial means it lost its old job, not every job.
